      4. Write `.deliverables.json` in the working directory listing every file the answer reports. The file is `{"files": [{"path": "<absolute path, or a path relative to the working directory>", "description": "<what the file shows>", "kind": "final"}]}`. `kind` is `"final"` for the results the answer presents and `"intermediate"` for supporting artifacts. When the task finishes the platform uploads the `"final"` files, replaces their paths in your answer with `data_entry:` links, and hands those links to the caller; `"intermediate"` files stay in the workspace for sibling agents. At least one listed file must be `"final"`, even when the task says not to publish files or that the caller will upload them. Refer to each final file in the answer by the same path you listed. Do not call `e14c.data_storage.upload()` yourself, even when the task asks for an upload or a URI. The manifest is bookkeeping: do not list it, copy it into output folders, or mention it or the upload in the answer.
      5. Call `submit_answer` when the success criteria are satisfied.
    </protocol>
    <success-criteria>
      - The task is answered with verifiable evidence from executed notebook results.
      - Data issues, assumptions, uncertainty, and limitations are reported.

The latter is the total time available to respond to that user message and resets whenever the user sends a new message. You will receive warnings when you approach the `total_execution_time` limit.

      Execution resource limits:
      - cpu limit: 7
      - memory limit: 23Gi

      Plan execution around these limits. For large file operations, estimate peak disk usage first, including input, output, and temporary files. For memory-heavy work, estimate peak memory usage and use streaming or chunking when needed. If a plan may exceed a limit, use a smaller plan. The memory budget applies to the Python kernel and all subprocesses it starts, combined. Never raise, disable, or bypass these limits. After an allocation failure, do not move the same allocation into a subprocess, background job, or worker pool to work around it. Retry only after reducing peak memory usage enough to fit the existing budget. If that is not possible, stop the computation and explain the limitation. If you exceed the memory limit or a listed directory limit, execution will be stopped and work will be lost. Trust the limits above over measurements: `os.cpu_count()` sees visible cores rather than your cpu quota, available-memory figures are static, and `shutil.disk_usage`/`statvfs` may report the backing filesystem rather than your quota. # The investor's view: what worries someone paying for open science (issue #380, round 2)

Sterling asked for a less-biased pass at the first round, written from the chair of someone deciding whether to
invest, with Edison as an independent check. This memo is that pass. The first round asked what open science is
*worth*. This one asks what someone who pays for it *gets back*, and what could go wrong.

**Start with:** the [bottom line](#bottom-line) and the [ranked concerns](#the-concerns-ranked). The supporting
files are the [pre-registration](PREREGISTRATION.md) (committed before any new data, in
[`80a45f4`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/commit/80a45f4)), the
[bias audit of the first round](BIAS_AUDIT.md), the [Edison answers](edison/) and the
[sourced 2025–26 evidence](evidence/ai_and_funding_evidence.md).

## Bottom line

**Open science is a good public investment and a hard private one.** For the three kinds of investor this memo
considers:

- **A venture investor in an open physical-science spin-out** (for example a company built on DAL) has the most to
  worry about. Openness gives away what such investors usually pay for: patents, exclusive data, protected
  designs. The customers who most want open tools are the ones with the least money. Edison, reading the first
  round's files from an investment committee's chair, wrote: *"I would not approve an investment on the case
  presented."*
- **A public-market investor in open-source software companies** has seen no premium. Every 2014–22 listing of an
  open-source-origin infrastructure company, failures and buyouts included, returned a median of 0.52 of what QQQ
  returned over the same window, against 0.84 for closed peers. That gap is mostly the timing of the listings:
  with listing-year controls it disappears. So the evidence shows **no premium and no proven penalty**.
- **A public funder** (DOE's Genesis Mission, ONR, NSF) wants the opposite of what the venture investor wants.
  Openness is the point. The funder's worry is that the lab isn't open *enough*: none of DAL's datasets has a DOI
  yet. Its other worry is that nobody will pay to maintain the work once the award ends.

The best investment case for openness is the narrow one. Open the parts that bring users in and make results
credible, such as drivers, methods and tooling. Keep, or file on, the parts customers pay for: compositions,
process windows, operating know-how, and the data that gives an edge for a while.

## How this round tried to be less biased

| Risk in round 1 | What this round did |
| --- | --- |
| The agent works for a lab that favours openness | Wrote the hypotheses and what would count against each **before** fetching any data, and committed them first ([pre-registration](PREREGISTRATION.md), [`80a45f4`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/commit/80a45f4)) |
| Famous examples stand in for the whole population | Took **every** listing of an open-source-origin company in 2014–22 and a closed cohort chosen by a category rule, with deal terms checked against filings and press releases ([verified terms](data/cohort_listings_verified.csv)) |
| The agent grades its own homework | Asked Edison nine questions worded neutrally and **without** the first round's conclusions ([queries](edison/queries.json)). Gave Edison the first round's brief and raw dataset and asked it to red-team them ([answer](edison/inv_redteam_round1_answer.md), [full review and code](edison/inv_redteam_round1_files/)) |
| Framing leaned one way | Audited the first round's framing ([`BIAS_AUDIT.md`](BIAS_AUDIT.md)) and stated the case *for* openness at its strongest ([below](#the-case-for-openness-stated-as-strongly-as-the-evidence-allows)) |
| Interested sources | Kept the venture-backed report, the advocacy studies and company statements, but labelled them as interested |

Independence is partial, and the limits are worth knowing. Edison retrieves and reads its own sources, but it may
run on models from the same handful of vendors, Claude included. The same agent wrote both rounds, and the same
person asked for both.

## Results against the pre-registered hypotheses

| # | Concern | What the data show | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H1 | Open-source origin doesn't earn public investors a premium | **Median value of $1 at the offer price, relative to $1 in QQQ: 0.52 (14 open-source listings) vs. 0.84 (25 closed).** Annualized, the median open-source listing trailed QQQ by 17.1 points a year and the median closed one by 2.9, a difference of −14.2 points (95% CI −25.1 to +2.2). Half the open-source listings (7 of 14) lost money from the offer price, against 9 of 25 closed ones. 10 of the 14 left the market through a buyout or merger: 6 at or below the offer price and 2 within 7% above it. With listing-year controls the gap goes away (ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.54–2.4): 7 of the 14 open-source listi
<...output truncated to 10000 characters (edit the cell to produce a shorter output if needed)...>
t answer 2 illustrates "who captures the value" with Databricks, the
   Hugging Face deal, Confluent, Red Hat and MongoDB. It doesn't put next to them the open-source companies
   whose public investors lost money or broke even: MariaDB, HashiCorp, SUSE, Couchbase, Cloudera and
   Hortonworks. Nor does it mention Docker, whose software became an industry standard and whose company was
   recapitalized. Picking cases by outcome flatters whatever strategy the winners used. H1 in
   [`INVESTOR_MEMO.md`](INVESTOR_MEMO.md) replaces the examples with every listing in a defined window.

3. **"Venture data agrees" rests on an interested source, and one of its numbers cuts the other way.** The
   7× and 14× exit medians come from a report co-written by a venture firm that invests in open source, a
   foundation and a trade group. The first round disclosed this but still led with the numbers. Exit medians
   are also conditional on an exit, and only 12% of the sample had one. The same report's 1.6× higher Series A
   valuation was presented as a strength. For an investor buying in, a higher entry price is a cost: it lowers
   the multiple unless exits are higher by more.

4. **"Foundations keep openness durable" is a commons argument, not an investment one.** Moving code to a
   neutral foundation (recommendation 2) is what keeps it open, and that is the point. It also gives up the
   control a company would need in order to relicense, bundle or exclude a competitor. Confluent could not
   relicense Kafka, and Kubernetes' largest earners are the clouds that host it.

5. **The report saw the investor's logic and recommended against it without weighing it.** Recommendation 3
   notes that "the 2025–26 AI-for-materials startups protect *data and compositions*" and that failed runs are
   "the signal closed players hoard". It then recommends releasing all data, failed runs included, within 12
   months. That can be the right call for a publicly funded lab. A spin-out would be giving away the asset
   its funders are paying for. The trade-off should be stated, not resolved by default.

6. **"Sell services around the open core" borrowed evidence from a different business.** Recommendation 4
   supports services with Databricks, Confluent and MongoDB Atlas, which are hosted software with software
   margins. Lab services, such as cloud-lab time, setup and integration, are a different business. Their
   track record in the case files is Strateos closing its hosted cloud lab in 2023, after about $80M or more
   in funding, and Emerald Cloud Lab, whose biggest win was a $40M cloud lab built for Carnegie Mellon.

7. **The dataset couldn't answer the investor's question, and that went unsaid.** The 179 case files were
   built to describe openness. Only 37 for-profit organizations have both a funding total and a value, almost
   none of them closed software companies, and organizations that failed mostly have no value recorded. Tested
   here (H2), openness shows no relationship with value per dollar raised (Spearman ρ −0.04, 95% CI −0.39 to
   0.31, n = 37). Neither side should claim the casebook as evidence.

## What was missing for an investor

- **Base rates.** Most venture-backed companies return less than the capital invested, open or closed. A
  strategy is judged by its whole distribution, including the companies nobody remembers.
- **Entry price and time.** Multiples on capital, internal rates of return and holding periods, not latest
  valuations. Private marks are not realized returns.
- **The customer's budget.** Open lab tools sell mostly to academic labs. US academic research is 55%
  federally funded ($64.6B of $117.7B in FY2024, NSF HERD), and federal science funding was cut and disrupted
  in 2025–26 (see the memo's H5).
- **Who else profits.** Open data and open models feed the largest firms first: the PDB trained AlphaFold, and
  Isomorphic Labs commercializes its successor, whose weights are not open for commercial use. The first round recorded this as a fact about the commons; for an
  investor it is the central risk.
- **The lab's own purchases.** By the first round's audit, the lab's alloy route runs on about 20 instruments,
  of which about 4 can be programmed. Its printers are closed Bambu Lab machines and its CALPHAD route uses
  proprietary Thermo-Calc. A lab that argues for openness still buys closed tools when they work better, which
  is exactly the willingness-to-pay question an investor would ask about an open product.

## What the first round got right, from an investor's chair

The audit is one-sided by design, so for balance:

- It said plainly that value goes "to whoever runs the service, owns the data or sells the hardware", that
  open hardware "pays in cost and longevity, not in valuation", and that the SDL-demo kit made $2.24 a kit.
- It disclosed the venture report's conflict of interest and the 12% exit rate.
- It corrected its own overstatements after review, in a public fourth video.

- **Red text (RGB: 255,0,0)**: External links to other files
- **Yellow background (RGB: 255,255,0)**: Key assumptions needing attention or cells that need to be updated

### Number Formatting Standards

#### Required Format Rules

- **Years**: Format as text strings (e.g., "2024" not "2,024")
- **Currency**: Use $#,##0 format; ALWAYS specify units in headers ("Revenue ($mm)")
- **Zeros**: Use number formatting to make all zeros "-", including percentages (e.g., "$#,##0;($#,##0);-")
- **Percentages**: Default to 0.0% format (one decimal)
- **Multiples**: Format as 0.0x for valuation multiples (EV/EBITDA, P/E)
- **Negative numbers**: Use parentheses (123) not minus -123

### Formula Construction Rules

#### Assumptions Placement

- Place ALL assumptions (growth rates, margins, multiples, etc.) in separate assumption cells
- Use cell references instead of hardcoded values in formulas
- Example: Use =B5*(1+$B$6) instead of =B5*1.05

#### Formula Error Prevention

- Verify all cell references are correct
- Check for off-by-one errors in ranges
- Ensure consistent formulas across all projection periods
- Test with edge cases (zero values, negative numbers)
- Verify no unintended circular references

#### Documentation Requirements for Hardcodes

- Comment or in cells beside (if end of table). Format: "Source: [System/Document], [Date], [Specific Reference], [URL if applicable]"
- Examples:
  - "Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]"
  - "Source: Company 10-Q, Q2 2025, Exhibit 99.1, [SEC EDGAR URL]"
  - "Source: Bloomberg Terminal, 8/15/2025, AAPL US Equity"
  - "Source: FactSet, 8/20/2025, Consensus Estimates Screen"
  - "Source: [3]" for a paper or web source listed on the "References" sheet. The `bibliography` skill shows how to build that sheet.

# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

## Overview

A user may ask you to create, edit, or analyze the contents of an .xlsx file. You have different tools and workflows available for different tasks.

## Reading and analyzing data

### Data analysis with pandas

For data analysis, visualization, and basic operations, use **pandas** which provides powerful data manipulation capabilities:

```python
import pandas as pd

# Read Excel
df = pd.read_excel("file.xlsx")  # Default: first sheet
all_sheets = pd.read_excel("file.xlsx", sheet_name=None)  # All sheets as dict

# Analyze
df.head()  # Preview data
df.info()  # Column info
df.describe()  # Statistics

# Write Excel
df.to_excel("output.xlsx", index=False)
```

## Excel File Workflows

## CRITICAL: Use Formulas, Not Hardcoded Values

**Always use Excel formulas instead of calculating values in Python and hardcoding them.** This ensures the spreadsheet remains dynamic and updateable.

### ❌ WRONG - Hardcoding Calculated Values

```python
# Bad: Calculating in Python and hardcoding result
total = df["Sales"].sum()
sheet["B10"] = total  # Hardcodes 5000

# Bad: Computing growth rate in Python
growth = (df.iloc[-1]["Revenue"] - df.iloc[0]["Revenue"]) / df.iloc[0]["Revenue"]
sheet["C5"] = growth  # Hardcodes 0.15

# Bad: Python calculation for average
avg = sum(values) / len(values)
sheet["D20"] = avg  # Hardcodes 42.5
```

### ✅ CORRECT - Using Excel Formulas

```python
# Good: Let Excel calculate the sum
sheet["B10"] = "=SUM(B2:B9)"

# Good: Growth rate as Excel formula
sheet["C5"] = "=(C4-C2)/C2"

# Good: Average using Excel function
sheet["D20"] = "=AVERAGE(D2:D19)"
```

This applies to ALL calculations - totals, percentages, ratios, differences, etc. The spreadsheet should be able to recalculate when source data changes.

## Common Workflow

1. **Choose tool**: pandas for data, openpyxl for formulas/formatting
2. **Create/Load**: Create new workbook or load existing file
3. **Modify**: Add/edit data, formulas, and formatting
4. **Save**: Write to file

### Creating new Excel files

```python
# Using openpyxl for formulas and formatting
from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font, PatternFill, Alignment

wb = Workbook()
sheet = wb.active

# Add data
sheet["A1"] = "Hello"
sheet["B1"] = "World"
sheet.append(["Row", "of", "data"])

# Add formula
sheet["B2"] = "=SUM(A1:A10)"

# Formatting
sheet["A1"].font = Font(bold=True, color="FF0000")
sheet["A1"].fill = PatternFill("solid", start_color="FFFF00")
sheet["A1"].alignment = Alignment(horizontal="center")

# Column width
sheet.column_dimensions["A"].width = 20

wb.save("output.xlsx")
```

### Editing existing Excel files

```python
# Using openpyxl to preserve formulas and formatting
from openpyxl import load_workbook

# Load existing file
wb = load_workbook("existing.xlsx")
sheet = wb.active  # or wb['SheetName'] for specific sheet

# Working with multiple sheets
for sheet_name in wb.sheetnames:
    sheet = wb[sheet_name]
    print(f"Sheet: {sheet_name}")

# Modify cells
sheet["A1"] = "New Value"
sheet.insert_rows(2)  # Insert row at position 2
sheet.delete_cols(3)  # Delete column 3

# Add new sheet
new_sheet = wb.create_sheet("NewSheet")
new_sheet["A1"] = "Data"

wb.save("modified.xlsx")
```

## Formula Verification Checklist

Quick checks to ensure formulas work correctly:

### Essential Verification

- [ ] **Test 2-3 sample references**: Verify they pull correct values before building full model
- [ ] **Column mapping**: Confirm Excel columns match (e.g., column 64 = BL, not BK)
- [ ] **Row offset**: Remember Excel rows are 1-indexed (DataFrame row 5 = Excel row 6)

### Common Pitfalls

- [ ] **NaN handling**: Check for null values with `pd.notna()`
- [ ] **Far-right columns**: FY data often in columns 50+
- [ ] **Multiple matches**: Search all occurrences, not just first
- [ ] **Division by zero**: Check denominators before using `/` in formulas (#DIV/0!)
- [ ] **Wrong references**: Verify all cell references point to intended cells (#REF!)
- [ ] **Cross-sheet references**: Use correct format (Sheet1!A1) for linking sheets

### Formula Testing Strategy

- [ ] **Start small**: Test formulas on 2-3 cells before applying broadly
- [ ] **Verify dependencies**: Check all cells referenced in formulas exist
- [ ] **Test edge cases**: Include zero, negative, and very large values

## Best Practices

### Library Selection

- **pandas**: Best for data analysis, bulk operations, and simple data export
- **openpyxl**: Best for complex formatting, formulas, and Excel-specific features

### Working with openpyxl

- Cell indices are 1-based (row=1, column=1 refers to cell A1)
- Use `data_only=True` to read calculated values: `load_workbook('file.xlsx', data_only=True)`
- **Warning**: If opened with `data_only=True` and saved, formulas are replaced with values and permanently lost
- For large files: Use `read_only=True` for reading or `write_only=True` for writing
- Formulas are preserved but not evaluated by openpyxl

### Working with pandas

- Specify data types to avoid inference issues: `pd.read_excel('file.xlsx', dtype={'id': str})`
- For large files, read specific columns: `pd.read_excel('file.xlsx', usecols=['A', 'C', 'E'])`
- Handle dates properly: `pd.read_excel('file.xlsx', parse_dates=['date_column'])`

## Code Style Guidelines

**IMPORTANT**: When generating Python code for Excel operations:

- Write minimal, concise Python code without unnecessary comments
- Avoid verbose variable names and redundant operations
- Avoid unnecessary print statements

**For Excel files themselves**:

- Add comments to cells with complex formulas or important assumptions
- Document data sources for hardcoded values
- Include notes for key calculations and model sections

# The investor's view: what worries someone paying for open science (issue #380, round 2)

Sterling asked for a less-biased pass at the first round, written from the chair of someone deciding whether to
invest, with Edison as an independent check. This memo is that pass. The first round asked what open science is
*worth*. This one asks what someone who pays for it *gets back*, and what could go wrong.

**Start with:** the [bottom line](#bottom-line) and the [ranked concerns](#the-concerns-ranked). The supporting
files are the [pre-registration](PREREGISTRATION.md) (committed before any new data, in
[`80a45f4`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/commit/80a45f4)), the
[bias audit of the first round](BIAS_AUDIT.md), the [Edison answers](edison/) and the
[sourced 2025–26 evidence](evidence/ai_and_funding_evidence.md).

## Bottom line

**Open science is a good public investment and a hard private one.** For the three kinds of investor this memo
considers:

- **A venture investor in an open physical-science spin-out** (for example a company built on DAL) has the most to
  worry about. Openness gives away what such investors usually pay for: patents, exclusive data, protected
  designs. The customers who most want open tools are the ones with the least money. Edison, reading the first
  round's files from an investment committee's chair, wrote: *"I would not approve an investment on the case
  presented."*
- **A public-market investor in open-source software companies** has seen no premium. Every 2014–22 listing of an
  open-source-origin infrastructure company, failures and buyouts included, returned a median of 0.52 of what QQQ
  returned over the same window, against 0.84 for closed peers. That gap is mostly the timing of the listings:
  with listing-year controls it disappears. So the evidence shows **no premium and no proven penalty**.
- **A public funder** (DOE's Genesis Mission, ONR, NSF) wants the opposite of what the venture investor wants.
  Openness is the point. The funder's worry is that the lab isn't open *enough*: none of DAL's datasets has a DOI
  yet. Its other worry is that nobody will pay to maintain the work once the award ends.

The best investment case for openness is the narrow one. Open the parts that bring users in and make results
credible, such as drivers, methods and tooling. Keep, or file on, the parts customers pay for: compositions,
process windows, operating know-how, and the data that gives an edge for a while.

## How this round tried to be less biased

| Risk in round 1 | What this round did |
| --- | --- |
| The agent works for a lab that favours openness | Wrote the hypotheses and what would count against each **before** fetching any data, and committed them first ([pre-registration](PREREGISTRATION.md), [`80a45f4`](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/commit/80a45f4)) |
| Famous examples stand in for the whole population | Took **every** listing of an open-source-origin company in 2014–22 and a closed cohort chosen by a category rule, with deal terms checked against filings and press releases ([verified terms](data/cohort_listings_verified.csv)) |
| The agent grades its own homework | Asked Edison nine questions worded neutrally and **without** the first round's conclusions ([queries](edison/queries.json)). Gave Edison the first round's brief and raw dataset and asked it to red-team them ([answer](edison/inv_redteam_round1_answer.md), [full review and code](edison/inv_redteam_round1_files/)) |
| Framing leaned one way | Audited the first round's framing ([`BIAS_AUDIT.md`](BIAS_AUDIT.md)) and stated the case *for* openness at its strongest ([below](#the-case-for-openness-stated-as-strongly-as-the-evidence-allows)) |
| Interested sources | Kept the venture-backed report, the advocacy studies and company statements, but labelled them as interested |

Independence is partial, and the limits are worth knowing. Edison retrieves and reads its own sources, but it may
run on models from the same handful of vendors, Claude included. The same agent wrote both rounds, and the same
person asked for both.

## Results against the pre-registered hypotheses

| # | Concern | What the data show | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H1 | Open-source origin doesn't earn public investors a premium | **Median value of $1 at the offer price, relative to $1 in QQQ: 0.52 (14 open-source listings) vs. 0.84 (25 closed).** Annualized, the median open-source listing trailed QQQ by 17.1 points a year and the median closed one by 2.9, a difference of −14.2 points (95% CI −25.1 to +2.2). Half the open-source listings (7 of 14) lost money from the offer price, against 9 of 25 closed ones. 10 of the 14 left the market through a buyout or merger: 6 at or below the offer price and 2 within 7% above it. With listing-year controls the gap goes away (ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.54–2.4): 7 of the 14 open-source listings came in 2021–22 | **Concern stands** (the pre-registered test needed open 
<...output truncated to 10000 characters (edit the cell to produce a shorter output if needed)...>
mous-lab services ("alloys as a service") | Throughput, validated measurements, turnaround | **Neutral to helpful.** Open methods build trust, and the value is in operating the lab | Strateos (folded 2023), Emerald Cloud Lab (survived), Radical AI (a closed alloy SDL with open simulation tools) |
| Orchestration software and drivers | Hosted orchestration, support, integrations | **Helps adoption, hurts capture**, unless the hosted layer stays closed. OEMs and AI platforms may set the standards | Opentrons (open API, hardware revenue), Atinary (closed), PyLabRobot (open, no company) |

**The funder sees a different gap.** For DOE's Genesis Mission or ONR, openness is a requirement, not a risk. The
first round's [DAL audit](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/blob/db24bf3/outputs/issue-380-open-science-ai/dal/dal_openness_audit.md)
found that no lab dataset has a DOI yet, that sensor and run records sit in a private database, and that the
rePowder's process data can't be exported. To a public funder the lab is **not open enough**. To a venture
investor in a spin-out it may be **too open**. A written rule that separates the two (file, then publish; embargo
periods; which layer is open) serves both.

**The SDL-demo kit is not a venture investment, and that's fine.** At $80 a kit with a stated $2.24 profit, it
needs about ten times the price or a service around it to fund one engineer. It earns its keep as teaching and
outreach. Grants and partners such as GroupGets are the right money for it. Edison adds a fair caveat: one kit's
margin doesn't prove that services beat hardware, because bespoke integration services can have worse economics.

## Where Edison agreed and disagreed

**Agreed** (each reached on its own):

- There is no openness premium in the case files. Edison's statistics on the same 37 rows match this memo's
  exactly.
- Public value is not shareholder value.
- The 7× and 14× venture medians are not an expected return.
- The 87% hardware saving is not an installed-cost comparison.
- Surviving forks show the commons is durable, not that a company captured value.

**Edison went further than this memo:**

- It would not approve the investment as presented.
- It ranked "discovery doesn't transfer to manufacturable alloys" and "integration and support destroy margins"
  third and fourth.
- It could not reproduce the first round's "10 of 15 closing moves came at or after an acquisition". It found 7 of
  14 dated moves.

**Edison pushed back on the bear case:**

- AI also returns value to the commons (the AlphaFold database).
- Coding assistants raise contributions.
- The $2.24 kit margin proves little about services.
- On the precedent question, it counted Opentrons as a qualified open-hardware company worth $1B or more, where
  the first round's case file treats Opentrons' current hardware as closed.

## Limits

- **Small samples.** H1 has 39 listings. None of its differences is significant at 95%, and listing vintage
  explains most of the gap.
- **The rules are mine.** The closed cohort's category rule was written before returns were computed, but other
  reasonable rules exist. The [sensitivity runs](data/h1_summary.csv) add the companies found after
  pre-registration (Instructure ×2, ForgeRock, Tenable; UiPath, C3.ai, Amplitude). They narrow the gap to −8.0
  points a year (95% CI −17.9 to +10.7). The four added offer prices came from memory: the session's web-search
  budget ran out before they could be checked against filings.
- **Public markets are not venture returns.** The listing cohort covers companies that reached an IPO. The private
  failures behind them remain uncounted, the gap Edison calls decisive.
- **Recent facts.** Many 2025–26 facts come from company statements and news. Each is labelled
  [confirmed] or [unconfirmed] in the [evidence file](evidence/ai_and_funding_evidence.md).
- **Severity rankings are judgments.** They are informed by Edison's independent ranking but not derived from data.

## Files

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [`PREREGISTRATION.md`](PREREGISTRATION.md) | Hypotheses and tests, committed before the data |
| [`BIAS_AUDIT.md`](BIAS_AUDIT.md) | Where the first round leaned toward openness |
| [`edison/`](edison/) | Nine round-1 Edison jobs: answers, references and full trajectories. The red team's report, code and tables are in [`inv_redteam_round1_files/`](edison/inv_redteam_round1_files/) |
| [`evidence/ai_and_funding_evidence.md`](evidence/ai_and_funding_evidence.md) | Dated, sourced 2025–26 evidence on AI and open source, US science funding and relicensing |
| [`data/cohort_listings_verified.csv`](data/cohort_listings_verified.csv) | Offer prices, deal terms, first-day closes and sources for 43 listings |
| `data/h1_*.csv`, `data/h2_*.csv`, `data/fundamentals_*.csv` | Results tables |
| [`scripts/`](scripts/) | Every script, run from this folder with the Python 3.12 venv (see [`README.md`](README.md)) |
| [`figures/`](figures/) | Charts |

| H6 | Open-by-default disclosure lowers a physical-science spin-out's ability to raise money | Causal studies of patents and startup financing; novelty and grace-period rules | Evidence that patents don't matter for financing in these sectors, or that openness raises financing |

  listed 2014–2022. Planned list: Hortonworks, Talend, MuleSoft, Cloudera, MongoDB, Pivotal, Elastic, Confluent,

- **Closed cohort:** closed-source companies listed on a US exchange 2014–2022 in the same product categories:

  operations, and infrastructure software. Security, business applications (CRM, HR, finance), consumer and
  hardware companies are excluded. The list is drawn from Wikipedia's and Renaissance Capital's IPO records before
  any returns are computed, and every qualifying company is kept, whatever it later did.
- **Returns:** offer price to the cash deal price on the closing date, or to the latest close for companies still
  listed. Stock-and-cash deals are valued at the announced value per share. Spin-offs and special dividends are
  included where Yahoo's adjusted prices capture them, and noted otherwise. A second version starts from the
  first-day close, which is what a public investor could actually pay.

(`edison/queries.json`). One analysis job then receives the first round's brief, recommendations and dataset and
is asked to red-team them. A second analysis job will red-team this round's own memo before it is final. Edison's
answers are kept in full and reported separately from my own conclusions, including where they disagree.

77:   Openness hands the core to competitors and customers.
78: - **Evidence for.** Firms would need **$8.8T** to replace the open-source software they use, which cost
79:   **$4.15B** to write (Hoffmann, Nagle & Zhou 2024). Commercial open-source companies are worth about $375B
80:   together. AWS sold managed Elasticsearch, and Elastic's own employees wrote over 95% of its code changes
81:   (Edison, [COSS evidence](edison/inv_coss_financial_evidence_answer.md)). In the physical sciences, the PDB's open
82:   structures trained AlphaFold, and Isomorphic Labs commercializes its successor. Edison's red team ranked this
83:   concern first.
84: - **Evidence against.** Red Hat ($34B), MongoDB and Databricks show capture is possible when the company runs
85:   something scarce alongside the open code: a hosted service, support, certification. Edison's AI answer notes that
86:   value also flows back: DeepMind funds the open AlphaFold database of over 214M structures.
87: - **Ask in diligence.** What do customers pay for that stays scarce *after* the code, designs and data are public?
88: 
89: ### 2. The customers who want open tools have the least money
90: 
91: - **The concern.** Open lab tools sell mainly to academic labs. Those labs pick them because they are cheap, run on
92:   grant cycles, and need support that the low price doesn't cover.
93: - **Evidence for.** US universities spent $117.7B on R&D in FY2024, 55% of it federal (NSF HERD). FY2025–26 brought
94:   grant terminations, a 20.5% drop in NIH competing grants, and NSF awards down 43% from FY2024 to FY2026. Agilent
95:   reports US labs "using available funding to keep their labs running as opposed to investing in new capital
96:   equipment" ([evidence](evidence/ai_and_funding_evidence.md#b-us-federal-science-funding)). The open-hardware
97:   literature describes academic demand as fragmented, grant-dependent and price-driven
98:   ([Edison](edison/inv_open_hardware_risks_answer.md)). Two of this lab's own data points:
99:   - The $80 SDL-demo kit made a stated **$2.24 a kit**.
100:   - The Acceleration Consortium lab *bought* equipment and never sold any
101:     ([first round](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/blob/db24bf3/outputs/issue-380-open-science-ai/gh-mining/commercialization_digest.md)).
102: - **Evidence against.**
103:   - Congress largely held FY2026 appropriations flat, and the 15% indirect-cost caps are blocked.
104:   - Big tools makers have small academic exposure (Danaher under 5%, Revvity about 5%), and Bruker saw US
105:     academic demand strengthen in Q3 2026.
106:   - Industrial customers exist: early cloud labs sold mainly to industry, at over $100k a method.
107: - **Ask in diligence.** What share of revenue comes from non-academic customers who reorder?
108: 
109: ### 3. Publishing first forfeits the patents that unlock financing
110: 
111: - **The concern.** In materials, chemistry and devices, patents are financing instruments as much as legal ones.
112: - **Evidence for.**
113:   - Patents' effect is causal: a first patent raises a startup's chance of venture funding by 47%, its
114:     five-year employment growth by 55% and its sales growth by 80% (Farre-Mensa, Hegde & Ljungqvist 2020).
115:   - Pending patents signalled quality to investors in 370 semiconductor startups (Hsu & Ziedonis 2013).
116:   - Europe has absolute novelty, so a preprint or an open repository forfeits European rights for good.
117:   - Open-source engagement had no net effect on funding in highly competitive markets (Conti et al. 2021).
118:   - All via [Edison](edison/inv_disclosure_ip_physsci_answer.md).
119: - **Evidence against.**
120:   - The US one-year grace period exists.
121:   - File-then-publish (patent–paper pairs) lets a lab publish and patent at once.
122:   - Tacit know-how and execution speed protect complex physical processes even without patents.
123: - **Ask in diligence.**
124:   - Is there a written rule for what gets filed before it is published?
125:   - Who owns the IP: the university, the funder, or the inventors?
126: 
127: ### 4. Openness doesn't fix hardware economics; it removes the protection
128: 
129: - **The concern.** Hardware ties up cash in tooling, inventory, certification and support, and clones undercut
130:   open designs.
131: - **Evidence for.**
132:   - Open-hardware firms that last are bootstrapped and mid-sized: SparkFun had about $30M of revenue in 2013, and
133:     Prusa about $157M in 2024. Edison's summary: "a profitable small-to-medium enterprise rather than a
134:     venture-scale exit".
135:   - LulzBot grew fast, stayed fully open, and collapsed in 2019. Prusa restricted its newes

Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/citation-integrity

- Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or a subagent task.
- Every primary source needs a full BibTeX entry. Cite from the BibTeX, not from a narrative answer.
- Never cite yourself or guess citations from memory.

## Web sources

Every source you use from the `e14c.web` tools needs a full BibTeX entry.

- When you write an entry yourself, name its key with the first author's surname, the year, and the first word of the title, for example `jumper2021highly`. This keeps keys unique.
- Save each entry with `e14c.web.save_citation(bibtex)` as soon as you use the source. It appends the entry to your own file in the project's citations folder, `$WORKSPACE_PATH/citations/$PROJECT_ID/$TRAJECTORY_ID.bib`. In a chat session, `TRAJECTORY_ID` is the session ID. Do not write citation files any other way.

### Sources with a DOI

Call `await e14c.web.cite_doi(doi)`. It fetches the BibTeX from doi.org and saves it. This works for Crossref and DataCite DOIs, including arXiv DOIs such as `10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762`. Check that the title and authors in the returned entry match the paper you read.

### Sources without a DOI

Write the BibTeX entry yourself. Take every field from the source, never from memory.

- Use `@online` for web pages, database records, datasets, software, and reports. The report template hides URLs for most entry types, but it always prints them for `@online`, so readers can find the source.
- Include `author`, `title`, `url`, and `urldate`. `urldate` is the date you accessed the page, written as `YYYY-MM-DD`. Add `date` when the page shows a publication or update date.
- When there is no personal author, put the organization in `author` inside double braces, such as `{{UniProt Consortium}}`. The double braces stop it from being split into first and last names. Use the organization's short name in the key.
- When the page has no date, use the access year in the key.
- Many scholarly pages list their title, authors, and date in `citation_*` meta tags. `(await e14c.web.fetch_page(url)).text` returns the raw HTML so you can read them.
- In `title`, escape `&`, `%`, `_`, and `#` with a backslash, and wrap acronyms in braces to keep their capitals. Do not escape anything in `url`.
- For a journal article with no DOI, use `@article` with `journal`, `volume`, `number`, `pages`, and `year` instead. These fields let a reader find it without a link.

```bibtex
@online{uniprot2026uniprotkb,
  author  = {{UniProt Consortium}},
  title   = {{UniProtKB} entry {P04637} ({P53\_HUMAN}): Cellular tumor antigen p53},
  url     = {https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P04637/entry},
  urldate = {2026-10-12},
}
```

[Appended Cell #5] [stdout]
# Dated evidence: AI and the open-source funnel, US federal science funding, investor sentiment

Gathered 2026-11-25 by a research sub-agent for the investor memo, with instructions to include evidence against each
concern as well as for it. **[confirmed]** means the number was seen in the opened source (page, PDF, or the GitHub,
Stack Exchange or npm API); **[unconfirmed]** means it was seen only in a search snippet or secondary write-up. The
session's web-search budget ran out partway through section C, so C1 is thin.

## A. AI and the open-source business funnel

### A1. Tailwind Labs
- Adam Wathan, GitHub comment 2026-01-07: "75% of the people on our engineering team lost their jobs here yesterday because of the brutal impact AI has had on our business." (https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss.com/pull/2388#issuecomment-3717222957) [confirmed]
- Same comment: "Traffic to our docs is down about 40% from early 2023 despite Tailwind being more popular than ever. The docs are the only way people find out about our commercial products." [confirmed]
- Same comment: "Tailwind is growing faster than it ever has and is bigger than it ever has been, and our revenue is down close to 80%." [confirmed]
- He closed the PR that would have added LLM-friendly docs (/llms.txt): "I'm nervous to offer them without solving that problem first." [confirmed]
- Runway, quoted by DevClass 2026-01-08: "if nothing changed, then in about six months we would no longer be able to meet payroll obligations." (https://www.devclass.com/ai-ml/2026/01/08/tailwind-labs-lays-off-75-percent-of-its-engineers-thanks-to-brutal-impact-of-ai/4079571) [confirmed]
- Podcast 2026-02-18: the cuts were "three of the four engineers"; the company is bootstrapped; after the layoffs "we added a lot of partner program revenue", which he calls "charity as a business"; he calls AI "the most transformative thing I've used for building things." (https://tighten.com/insights/pragmatic-ai-ep2-adam-wathan-ai-impact-on-open-source-funding/) [confirmed]
- New sponsors after the layoffs (amounts undisclosed): Vercel, Google AI Studio, Lovable, Supabase, Gumroad. (https://analyticsindiamag.com/ai-features/tailwind-was-crushed-by-ai-now-ai-companies-are-rescuing-it, 2026-01-24) [confirmed; secondary]
- npm monthly downloads of `tailwindcss`: 19.9M (Jan 2023), 49.9M (Jan 2025), 122.3M (Dec 2025), 631.9M (Oct 2026). (https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/2026-10-01:2026-10-31/tailwindcss) [confirmed]. Caveat: `react` went from 119M to 887M a month and `next` from 34M to 320M over the same span; automated and agent installs inflate downloads, so they don't measure users.

### A2. Stack Overflow
- del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva & Wachs, *PNAS Nexus* 3(9), 2024-09-11: posting fell about 25% within six months of ChatGPT relative to Russian- and Chinese-language counterparts and maths forums; a lower bound; larger for the most widely used languages. (https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/3/9/pgae400/7754871) [confirmed]
- Burtch, Lee & Chen, *Scientific Reports* (May 2024): visits and questions fell, most on topics where ChatGPT does well; Reddit communities showed no decline; the loss was concentrated among newer users. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-61221-0) [unconfirmed]
- Monthly questions, Stack Exchange API (excludes deleted questions; queried 2026-11-25): Mar 2014 207,169; Nov 2022 109,119; Dec 2023 42,280; Dec 2024 17,913; Dec 2025 4,114; Oct 2026 843 (−99.2% vs Nov 2022). Annual: 2022 1,334,585; 2023 787,547; 2024 398,312; 2025 108,909; Jan–Oct 2026 19,571. The decline began before ChatGPT: −47% from Mar 2014 to Nov 2022. [confirmed]
- Prosus FY2026 results (year to 2026-03-31): Stack Overflow revenue rose from $115M to $129M (+12%), adjusted EBITDA from −$9M to +$12M; the group took $482M of impairments "primarily related to Stack Overflow and GoodHabitz", "following the disruption caused by generative AI." (https://www.prosus.com/~/media/Files/P/prosus-corp-v2/results-reports-and-events-archive/annual-report/2026/prosus-financial-results-fy26-booklet.pdf) [confirmed]
- Earlier Stack Overflow impairments: $246M, $560M and $372M (2023–24), about $1.178B, 68% of the $1.742B purchase price. (https://www.citizen.co.za/business/how-ai-decimated-this-prosus-company/, 2026-02-05) [confirmed; secondary]

### A3. Other traffic that funds open projects
- Wikipedia human pageviews down about 8% for Mar–Aug 2025 vs 2024 after reclassifying evasive bots; Wikimedia blames AI answers in search and social video and warns of fewer volunteers and donors. (https://diff.wikimedia.org/2025/10/17/new-user-trends-on-wikipedia/) [confirmed]
- Mintlify (docs host, vendor data): AI coding agents 45.3% of docs requests vs browsers 45.8% over 30 days (https://www.mintlify.com/blog/state-of-ai, 2026-04-03); in August 2026, 257M agent requests vs 131M human page loads (https://www.mintlify.com/blog/the-state-of-knowledge-2026-highlights, 2026-09-16). [confirmed]
- 
<...output truncated to 10000 characters (edit the cell to produce a shorter output if needed)...>
search-grant dollars +3.0% to $26.503B, partly from funding grants up front. (https://www.grants.nih.gov/news-events/nih-extramural-nexus-news/2026/03/fiscal-year-2025-by-the-numbers-extramural-grant-investments-in-research) [confirmed]
- JAMA study: 694 NIH grants worth about $1.8B terminated in about a month in spring 2025. (https://www.statnews.com/2025/05/08/trump-nih-cuts-jama-study-analyzes-1-point-8-billion-in-grant-cancellations/) [confirmed]
- CRS: as of 2026-04-10, 1,392 NIH awards terminated ($539M unspent obligations), many later reinstated; fewer than 6 midstream terminations 2012–Jan 2025. (https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2026-04-17_IF13131_c620ea761ed58004260034c2b14c614accfa0b17.pdf) [confirmed]
- 15% cap: NIH's permanently blocked (injunction 2025-04-04, affirmed 2026-01-05, no Supreme Court petition); DOE rescinded its caps effective 2026-01-23; NSF's vacated 2025-06-20 [unconfirmed]; FY2026 laws bar changes to NIH indirect-cost policy. OMB's proposed Uniform Guidance rewrite (2026-05-29) has no cap but prefers "institutions with lower indirect cost rates". (https://www.aamc.org/about-us/biomedical-research/science-policy-hub/federal-research-related-litigation; https://www.asme.org/government-relations/policy-impact/energy-department-rescinds-implementation-of-indirect-cost-policy; https://www.gtlaw.com/en/insights/2026/7/omb-proposes-significant-revisions-to-the-uniform-guidance-for-grants-and-agreements) [confirmed]

### B3. Tools companies' academic and government exposure
- **Bruker:** US academia and government "about 8% of our revenue", NIH-funded "only 3% to 4%" (2025-03-12); FY2025 revenue $3.44B, −3.7% organic, citing "headwinds from academic funding"; the FY2025 10-K calls the cuts "a material adverse effect" on its US academic business; it sold 2 GHz-class NMR systems in 2025 vs 4 in 2024; in Q3 2026 it saw demand strengthening "in Q3 also in the US academic market". (https://ir.bruker.com/press-releases/press-release-details/2026/Bruker-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx; https://s22.q4cdn.com/617463959/files/doc_downloads/2026/03/BRKR_10K_123125.pdf; https://finviz.com/news/415261/bruker-reports-third-quarter-2026-financial-results) [confirmed]
- **Thermo Fisher:** academic and government "declined in the low single digits" in Q4 and full-year 2025; 2026 guidance assumes "similar conditions". (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/01/29/thermo-fisher-tmo-q4-2025-earnings-transcript/) [confirmed]
- **Danaher:** direct NIH sales under 1% of revenue, total academic exposure under 5%. [confirmed]
- **Agilent:** academia and government is its smallest end market; −8% in fiscal Q1 2026 and −5% in Q2; US labs are "using available funding to keep their labs running as opposed to investing in new capital equipment". (https://s24.q4cdn.com/305549747/files/doc_earnings/2026/q1/transcript/Q1-26-Prepared-Remarks-Final.pdf) [confirmed]
- **Waters:** academic and government flat for FY2025 (−1% constant currency). [confirmed]
- **Revvity:** academia about 5% of revenue, NIH about 1%. [confirmed]
- **Bio-Techne:** academic customers about 21% of revenue, US institutions about 12%. [confirmed]
- **Illumina:** CEO 2026-01-14: "we still think 2026 will be muted on the research in [the] academic environment." [confirmed]

## C. Investor sentiment and relicensing, 2024–2026
- Prosus wrote down Stack Overflow for "the disruption caused by generative AI" (results dated 2026-06-27). [confirmed]
- Menlo Ventures: open-source share of enterprise AI model use fell "from 19% last year to 11% today" (2025-12-09). (https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/) [confirmed]
- Accel on Supabase: "We haven't seen a company grow at this pace, certainly in the database layer, ever before" (2026-06-04). [confirmed]
- Heather Meeker, 2026-04-09: "copyleft is moribund"; "maintaining a fork is almost always more expensive and difficult than complying." (https://heathermeeker.com/tag/lgpl/) [confirmed]
- Redis added AGPL for Redis 8 (2025-05-01); its CEO said the 2024 switch "hurt our relationship with the Redis community" and that "AWS and Google now maintain their own fork." (https://redis.io/blog/agplv3/) [confirmed]
- Elastic added AGPL (2024-08-29). (https://www.elastic.co/blog/elasticsearch-is-open-source-again) [confirmed]
- Liquibase 5.0 moved from Apache 2.0 to the source-available Functional Source License (2025-09-30). [confirmed]
- MinIO wound down its open-source community edition: source-only releases (2025-10-15), maintenance mode (2025-12-03), repository archived (2026-02-12). (https://github.com/minio/minio) [confirmed]
- OpenAI released Apache-2.0 open-weight gpt-oss models (2025-08-05). [confirmed]
- Gaps: no direct 2024–26 statements from Sequoia, Redpoint, Bessemer or OSS Capital were found before the search budget ran out; no stock-price reactions to 2025–26 relicensings (the companies are private).

142: - **Ask in diligence.** What is the gross margin after support, calibration and warranty, and what does a clone
143:   cost to make?
144: 
145: ### 5. A discovery is not a product
146: 
147: - **The concern.** Autonomous labs generate candidates quickly. Customers pay for qualified materials, and
148:   qualifying them takes years.
149: - **Evidence for.**
150:   - Zymergen went from a ~$4.8B peak valuation to a ~$300M sale. Its first product had quality and marketing
151:     problems.
152:   - Toyota Research Institute spent ~$70M across 17 university projects (2017–25). Reported dead ends include a
153:     search that found no winning polymer and a cathode that decayed too quickly to sell.
154:   - A peer-reviewed reanalysis challenged the A-Lab's novelty claims.
155:   - Strateos abandoned its hosted cloud lab in 2023.
156:   - All via [Edison](edison/inv_lab_automation_outcomes_answer.md). In aerospace and defence, a new alloy takes
157:     years of qualification before anyone buys it at scale.
158: - **Evidence against.** Open methods and full provenance, failed runs included, make a discovery more credible.
159:   That can shorten a customer's own validation, which is a genuine argument for openness.
160: - **Ask in diligence.** Has anyone outside the lab reproduced a property improvement on production-relevant
161:   equipment?
162: 
163: ### 6. Public markets have not paid a premium for open-source origin
164: 
165: - **The concern.** If open source were a better model, it would show in returns.
166: - **Evidence.** H1 above.
167:   - Median value at the offer price relative to QQQ: 0.52 open-source vs. 0.84 closed.
168:   - Winners on both sides: MongoDB (12.9× from offer), Talend and MuleSoft (bought at 3.7× and 2.6×); Palantir,
169:     Cloudflare and Datadog.
170:   - Busts on both sides: MariaDB (−94.5%), Kaltura, HashiCorp (IBM paid $35 against an $80 IPO); Domo and Jamf.
171:   - Survivors look alike today (Yahoo, 2026-11-24, [summary](data/fundamentals_summary.csv)), median open-source
172:     vs. closed:
173:     - Gross margin: 76% vs. 76%.
174:     - Free-cash-flow margin: 27% vs. 25%.
175:     - EV/revenue: 6.0× vs. 6.2×.
176:     - Growth: 21% vs. 26%.
177:   - Edison found **no rigorous matched study** of open-source vs. proprietary company returns in the literature.
178:     It called the missing failure denominator "decisive".
179: - **Against.** With listing-year controls the gap disappears. The 2021–22 listings did badly whatever their licence.
180: - **Ask in diligence.** Compare against the entry price you are paying, not against the open-source winners.
181: 
182: ### 7. Licences are unstable, and closing later rarely pays
183: 
184: - **The concern.** Starting open and closing once competitors arrive is a common plan, and the evidence that it
185:   works is thin.
186: - **Evidence for.**
187:   - Edison's COSS answer cites an analyst who found "no evidence that relicensing improved the financial results
188:     of the vendors studied". Three of the four best-known relicensings drew forks (OpenSearch, OpenTofu, Valkey).
189:   - Elastic and Redis later added AGPL back. Redis's CEO said the switch "hurt our relationship with the Redis
190:     community", and AWS and Google now maintain their own fork.
191:   - MinIO archived its community edition in 2026. An AI-assisted rewrite moved chardet from LGPL to MIT.
192: - **Evidence against.** MongoDB's SSPL drew no comparable fork, and the market didn't punish it: +5.2% against QQQ
193:   in the five days after the announcement ([first round](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/blob/db24bf3/outputs/issue-380-open-science-ai/data/relicense_event_study.csv)).
194: - **Ask in diligence.** Choose the licence for the business you want in five years, not the one you have now, and
195:   hold trademarks and contributor agreements from day one.
196: 
197: ### 8. AI moves the value of open work to whoever runs the model
198: 
199: - **The concern.** AI answers questions without sending the visit. It trains on open code and data, and it makes
200:   re-implementation cheap. The open producer bears the costs and loses the funnel.
201: - **Evidence for.** All in the [evidence file](evidence/ai_and_funding_evidence.md#a-ai-and-the-open-source-business-funnel):
202:   - Tailwind: docs traffic −40%, revenue −80%, usage at a record.
203:   - Stack Overflow: questions −99% since November 2022, though they had already fallen 47% from 2014 to 2022.
204:     Its owner wrote off about $1.18B of it in 2023–24, and more in 2026.
205:   - Read the Docs: one AI crawler used 73 TB in a month.
206:   - Cloudflare's vinext covered 94% of Next.js's API for about $1,100 of AI tokens.
207:   - In the physical sciences, VASP's June 2026 rules bar AI training on its source (first round).
208: - **Evidence against.**
209:   - GitHub contributions +13% and merged PRs +29% (Octoverse 2025).

**e14c.web.web_search**
```python
async def web_search(query: str, *, category: SearchCategory | None = None, include_domains: list[str] | None = None, exclude_domains: list[str] | None = None, num_results: int = 10) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Search the web and return results with text and highlights.

    Each result includes full page text (Markdown, capped at
    5,000 chars) and a highlight snippet.

    Args:
        query: Natural language search query.
        category: Optional filter — ``company``, ``people``,
            ``scholarly``, ``news``, or ``financial``.
        include_domains: Restrict results to these domains.
        exclude_domains: Exclude results from these domains.
        num_results: Number of results (default 10, capped at 100).

    Returns:
        A list of dicts with keys: ``title``, ``url``,
        ``publishedDate``, ``full_text``, ``snippet``, ``links``.
    """
```

**e14c.web.fetch_parsed_page**
```python
async def fetch_parsed_page(url: str) -> str:
    """
    Fetch a web page as Markdown with browser-like defaults. May take up to 30 seconds for JS-heavy pages.

    Args:
        url: The URL to fetch.

    Returns:
        The page content as Markdown text.
    """
```

**e14c.web.save_citation**
```python
def save_citation(bibtex: str) -> Path:
    """
    Append a BibTeX entry for a web source to this agent's citations file.

    Each agent writes only to
    ``$WORKSPACE_PATH/citations/$PROJECT_ID/$TRAJECTORY_ID.bib``, so agents
    running in parallel never share a file. In chat sessions heron sets
    ``TRAJECTORY_ID`` to the session ID, so an orchestrator keeps one file
    across turns. ``e14c.citations.citation_files`` lists the ``.bib`` files
    in that directory.

    Example:
        save_citation(bibtex)  # from doi.org, or written by hand

    Returns:
        The path of the file the entry was appended to.
    """
```

**e14c.web.cite_doi**
```python
async def cite_doi(doi: str) -> str:
    """
    Fetch a work's BibTeX from doi.org and save it with ``save_citation``.

    Works for Crossref and DataCite DOIs, including arXiv DOIs such as
    ``10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762``.

    Example:
        entry = await cite_doi("10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2")

    Returns:
        The saved BibTeX entry. Check its title and authors against the work.
    """
```

Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/scientific-writing

# Scientific Writing

A report PDF is produced by compiling the Edison LaTeX template.

## 1. LaTeX setup

First, create a clean latex working directory, such as `latex_report/`.

Then, make two calls to fetch template latex files and build a bibliography.

### Download template files

```python
from e14c.reports.latex import fetch_edison_template

fetch_edison_template("latex_report")
```

This places the following in `latex_report/`:

- `template.tex` - loads arxiv package, additional default Edison styles, and document structure. Rename this to something more descriptive
- `arxiv.sty`
- `references.bib` - placeholder
- `edison-logo.pdf` - logo for the cover page (already configured in the template)

### House style lock

`template.tex` is a complete report with the house style already wired in - cover page, logo, colour palette, callout boxes, and the Data Sources table. Rename it, then fill it in: replace the `[REPLACE]` placeholders with your content and leave the `[KEEP]` blocks alone.

Compile that renamed copy as is - the preamble stays as fetched, the `[KEEP]` blocks stay where they are, and `arxiv.sty` is never edited. Fill the `[REPLACE]` placeholders and add sections between them; do not rebuild the document body around a cover page of your own. Depart from the house style only when the task explicitly says not to use the Edison template; adjectives like polished or demo-quality are not an opt-out.

If compile errors are in your content, fix the content. If they are in the template or `arxiv.sty`, report them; do not replace the template to get a clean compile.

### Build the bibliography

Build `latex_report/references.bib` as described in the `bibliography` skill. Load that skill first if it is not already loaded. It merges the literature task citations and the saved literature and web citation files into one file. The template's `\printbibliography` renders it.

Note: this overwrites anything in `references.bib`.

## 2. Drafting

### Skeleton

The orchestrator agent may have provided an outline of structural elements for the main text. Try to adhere to those. If the outline is ambiguous, here is an example

```
 1. Cover page
 2. Abstract / Executive Summary: one page max.
 3. Table of contents: long reports only (>= 10 pages). Omit for shorter reports.
 4. Introduction / Context: what is known, what the gap is.
 5. Methodology: reference trajectory/tasks as needed.
 6. Main content sections: organized by research question
 7. Recommendations (if needed): tiered near-, medium-, long-term
 8. Discussion / Caveats / Limitations: standalone or per-recommendation
 9. Conclusion: brief synthesis
10. Output provenance table: every asset to a real task UUID with a chat_url link
11. Bibliography: generated from references.bib via biblatex
```

## 3. Paper elements

Read the fetched template before drafting and reuse its approved patterns.

### Literature citations

Cite in-line using `\citep{key}`, or for multiple citations, `\citep{key1,key2}`. The template's `biblatex` (numbered style) handles rendering as `[N]` and truncates long author lists to the first 6 + "et al.".

The `template.tex` contains a command to render the bibliography.

### Edison trajectory citations

Any outputs of tasks (especially analyses tasks) that appear in the paper should be properly referenced to allow the reader to trace back to the originating trajectory. Ideal places to include these references include:

- The end of a figure/table legend
- Within a methods section
- Within a results section

Sub-agent outputs use the sub-agent's UUID, passed in via the dispatch. Outputs you produced yourself use `os.environ["TRAJECTORY_ID"]`. Never use `ORCHESTRATOR` or any placeholder string.

`\edtraj{<url>}{<short>}` renders `Edison: <short>` for inline trajectory references. Trajectory URLs should be obtained programmatically to reduce errors as follows:

```python
from e14c.subagents import chat_url

sub_url = chat_url("74d1ef6b-0f34-4805-ba2b-c110086e7e93")  # task (default)
self_url = chat_url()  # this trajectory
artifact_url = chat_url("report-pdf-ab12", kind="data_entry")  # uploaded artifact
```

For artifacts, wrap with href:

```latex
\href{<artifact_url>}{data\_entry:report-pdf-ab12}
```

See the template for how to update the Edison Platform Data Sources table.

### Tables and statistics

- Booktabs and alternating row shading on tables where it aids readability.
- Color-code priority programs.
- P-values appear alongside ORs/betas. No naked effect sizes. For discovery analyses, show only FDR-significant results.

### Figures

One overview figure per report.

- `e14c.image_generation.generate_image` for label-heavy scientific figures.
- `e14c.image_generation.generate_infographic` for non-text-heavy conceptual overviews.

You may also pass a reference image to edit.

Visual style: white or light background, muted palette (navy/black/gray), Nature-style, publication-ready. No chartjunk, no cartoon styling, no decoration. Every figure caption ends with the producing task UUID, hyperlinked via `chat_url` (see Edison trajectory citations above).

## 4. Pre-delivery validation

Complete the applicable checks before calling `submit_answer`.

### Build

- [ ] Compile the actual main `.tex` file with `tectonic`. Resolve compilation errors, undefined references, and alignment errors.
- [ ] Unless the task opted out of the house style, confirm the compiled file is the renamed template: the preamble differs from the fetched `template.tex` only by `[REPLACE]` substitutions, the `[KEEP]` blocks and the template cover page are intact, and `arxiv.sty` is unchanged. A hand-written preamble that loads `arxiv`, or a self-authored `titlepage` in place of the template cover, does not qualify.
- [ ] Confirm every `\citep{key}` resolves to an entry in `references.bib`.
- [ ] Include a table of contents only when the final PDF is at least 10 pages.
- [ ] Place `\FloatBarrier` or `\clearpage` before References so figures and tables cannot drift beyond it.

### Content and provenance

- [ ] Check every quantitative claim against the originating task output.
- [ ] Sweep the draft for claims with no citation. For each, either attach the source or restate it as explicit inference.
- [ ] Confirm figure and table captions, numbering, and in-text references agree.
- [ ] Ensure repeated values, ranked lists, scores, and entity sets are consistent across sections.
- [ ] Associate every task-derived asset with its originating task UUID and `chat_url`.
- [ ] Wrap artifact references using `chat_url(<id>, kind="data_entry")`.
- [ ] Upload every supporting file named for the reader and reference it with a `data_entry:` URI.
- [ ] Remove placeholders, draft or version labels, prior-iteration language, and inaccessible internal paths.
- [ ] Remove meta-context, including mentions of prompts, system internals, the orchestrator, or the document-generation process.

### Layout

- [ ] For new documents or changes that can affect layout, use `explore` to inspect every rendered PDF page for overflowing tables, clipped figures, misplaced floats, orphaned headings, blank pages, and excessive whitespace.
- [ ] For a targeted layout fix, inspect the affected pages again. Skip full layout inspection only for minor text edits unlikely to change pagination.

Run each applicable check once. If one fails, fix the issue and rerun only the affected checks. Submit when all applicable checks pass.

266: ## The case for openness, stated as strongly as the evidence allows
267: 
268: An unbiased memo has to give the other side its best case.
269: 
270: - **Open source produced some of the best outcomes in the cohort.** MongoDB returned 12.9× its offer price, about
271:   2.8 times QQQ over the same nine years. Talend and MuleSoft were bought at 3.7× and 2.6× their offer prices.
272:   Red Hat sold for $34B, and Databricks is the most valuable private software company in the case files.
273: - **At scale, open-source companies look like everyone else.** Their margins and valuation multiples match closed
274:   peers. Openness isn't a structural margin penalty once there is a hosted product.
275: - **Openness is distribution, and AI agents are a new distribution channel.** Supabase's growth comes from agents
276:   choosing an open default. Opentrons' open API made it the default robot in academic self-driving-lab builds, even
277:   after its hardware closed.
278: - **For a public funder, openness is the return.** The PDB costs about $6.9M a year and supports research worth far
279:   more (first round). NIH's open-access mandate raised patent citations to its research by 12–27%.
280: - **Open source threatens closed incumbents.** An event study found proprietary software stocks fell on the day of
281:   a Chinese open-model release (Edison, [COSS evidence](edison/inv_coss_financial_evidence_answer.md)). Investing
282:   only on the closed side carries its own risk.
283: - **Credibility is an asset in science.** Open methods and provenance, failed runs included, can make customers and
284:   regulators trust a result sooner.

127: ### 4. Openness doesn't fix hardware economics; it removes the protection
128: 
129: - **The concern.** Hardware ties up cash in tooling, inventory, certification and support, and clones undercut
130:   open designs.
131: - **Evidence for.**
132:   - Open-hardware firms that last are bootstrapped and mid-sized: SparkFun had about $30M of revenue in 2013, and
133:     Prusa about $157M in 2024. Edison's summary: "a profitable small-to-medium enterprise rather than a
134:     venture-scale exit".
135:   - LulzBot grew fast, stayed fully open, and collapsed in 2019. Prusa restricted its newest designs.
136:   - Bambu Lab, closed, took the consumer market. This lab bought Bambu printers.
137:   - Opentrons closed its hardware to scale ([case files](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/blob/db24bf3/outputs/issue-380-open-science-ai/companies/CASEBOOK.md)).
138: - **Evidence against.**
139:   - Closed hardware is no safe harbour either. Desktop Metal raised $438M and went bankrupt; Markforged went from
140:     a ~$2.1B SPAC valuation to a $42.5M resale; 3D Systems fell about 97% from its 2013 peak.
141:   - Hardware is hard whether open or closed. Openness mainly lowers the cost of being copied.
142: - **Ask in diligence.** What is the gross margin after support, calibration and warranty, and what does a clone
143:   cost to make?
208: - **Evidence against.**
209:   - GitHub contributions +13% and merged PRs +29% (Octoverse 2025).
210:   - Copilot raised OSS contributions 5.9% in one study and 28–40% in another.
211:   - Supabase's valuation doubled to $10B as agents chose it by default.
212:   - AI companies bought open-source teams (Anthropic–Bun, OpenAI–Astral) and now sponsor Tailwind.
213:   - curl's AI-slop problem eased by April 2026.
214:   - Edison's view: "shifts in bargaining power and unit economics, not evidence that openness has stopped creating
215:     value" ([answer](edison/inv_ai_age_open_economics_answer.md)).
216: - **Ask in diligence.** Does revenue depend on human attention, or on usage that AI agents generate?
217: 
218: ### 9. The numbers used to sell openness come from survivors and interested parties
219: 
220: - **The concern.** The headline evidence for open-source businesses is weak in ways that flatter it.
221: - **Evidence for.**
222:   - The 7× and 14× venture exit medians come from a report co-written by an open-source-focused VC, a foundation
223:     and a trade group. They are conditional on an exit, which only 12% of the sample had.
224:   - Edison adds that the report found **no statistically significant IPO capital-efficiency difference**, and that
225:     its exit-cohort description contains a date inconsistency ([red team](edison/inv_redteam_round1_answer.md)).
226:   - Only 2 of 118 commercial rows in the first round's case files record a shutdown or bankruptcy, so they cannot
227:     estimate failure rates.
228:   - Databricks alone is 51% of the commercial software value in those files.
229: - **Evidence against.** The academic estimates of value created (Hoffmann et al.; the NIH open-access study) are
230:   independent and careful. They measure social value, which is what a public funder buys.
231: - **Ask in diligence.** What is the full distribution, failures included, at your entry price?
232: 
233: ### 10. Who maintains it, and who buys it?
234: 
235: - **The concern.** Open projects depend on a few people. An acquirer pays for control, and open IP offers less to
236:   control.
237: - **Evidence for.**
238:   - 5% of developers produce about 96% of the value of widely used open source (Hoffmann et al.).
239:   - The xz backdoor came through a single overworked maintainer.
240:   - Of 191 research-data repositories that closed, 47% neither kept access nor named a successor (Strecker et al.,
241:     via [Edison](edison/inv_public_funding_dependence_answer.md)).
242:   - Exits for open hardware were small or undisclosed: Arduino went to Qualcomm at an undisclosed price, and
243:     LulzBot's assets were sold.
244:   - The AI-era open-source startups mostly sold to compute and chip companies, often as teams.
245: - **Evidence against.** Foundations keep projects alive through changes of owner (PyTorch, Kubernetes, Valkey).
246:   Strategic buyers do pay for open ecosystems: IBM paid $34B for Red Hat, $6.4B for HashiCorp and $11B for Confluent.
247: - **Ask in diligence.** Name three plausible acquirers and what each would be buying.
248: 
288: Drawn from Edison's red team ("what would change my assessment"), the IP literature and the cases above:
289: 
290: 1. **Name the scarce thing.** Say what customers will keep paying for after everything promised is public.
291:    Candidates are operating the lab (throughput and uptime), validated data for a period before release, hardware
292:    built to a quality standard, certification, workflow integration and a trademark.
293: 2. **File, then publish.** Keep a written rule: provisional patents on compositions and processes with a plausible
294:    licensee, filed before any preprint. Europe gives no grace period.
295: 3. **Open the complement, close the core.** Open drivers, schemas, methods and benchmarks. Close or embargo
296:    compositions, process windows and failure data for long enough to sell.
297: 4. **Paid demand from outside academia.** Pilots with independent industrial customers, then repeat purchases.
298:    Letters of interest and GitHub stars don't count.
299: 5. **Independent physical validation.** Property improvements reproduced across batches on production-relevant
300:    equipment, failures disclosed.
301: 6. **Fully burdened unit economics.** Support, calibration, downtime, consumables and the founders' unpaid labour
302:    included.
303: 7. **Signed legal clarity.** University assignment and licence, award obligations, vendor API rights and data rights.
304: 8. **Funding matched to the layer.** Grants and non-dilutive money for the open infrastructure; venture money only
305:    for the closed product.
306: 
307: ## DAL and the SDL kit, through each investor's eyes
308: 
309: **Which company would DAL be?** Edison's sharpest point is that "open orchestration on closed instruments describes
310: an architecture, not a validated business". There are three different businesses here, and openness affects each
311: differently:
312: 
313: | Possible company | What it sells | What openness does to it | Closest comparables |
314: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
315: | Alloy IP licensor | Exclusive rights to compositions and process windows | **Destroys the asset** unless filed before publication. Aerospace and defence licensees want exclusivity, given years of qualification | Closed AI-for-materials startups: Periodic Labs ($300M), CuspAI (over $650M) |
316: | Autonomous-lab services ("alloys as a service") | Throughput, validated measurements, turnaround | **Neutral to helpful.** Open methods build trust, and the value is in operating the lab | Strateos (folded 2023), Emerald Cloud Lab (survived), Radical AI (a closed alloy SDL with open simulation tools) |
317: | Orchestration software and drivers | Hosted orchestration, support, integrations | **Helps adoption, hurts capture**, unless the hosted layer stays closed. OEMs and AI platforms may set the standards | Opentrons (open API, hardware revenue), Atinary (closed), PyLabRobot (open, no company) |
318: 
319: **The funder sees a different gap.** For DOE's Genesis Mission or ONR, openness is a requirement, not a risk. The
320: first round's [DAL audit](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/byu-vcl/blob/db24bf3/outputs/issue-380-open-science-ai/dal/dal_openness_audit.md)
321: found that no lab dataset has a DOI yet, that sensor and run records sit in a private database, and that the
322: rePowder's process data can't be exported. To a public funder the lab is **not open enough**. To a venture
323: investor in a spin-out it may be **too open**. A written rule that separates the two (file, then publish; embargo
324: periods; which layer is open) serves both.
325: 
326: **The SDL-demo kit is not a venture investment, and that's fine.** At $80 a kit with a stated $2.24 profit, it
327: needs about ten times the price or a service around it to fund one engineer. It earns its keep as teaching and
328: outreach. Grants and partners such as GroupGets are the right money for it. Edison adds a fair caveat: one kit's
329: margin doesn't prove that services beat hardware, because bespoke integration services can have worse economics.

OSS value abstract
 Abstract

The value of a non-pecuniary (free) product is inherently difficult to assess. A pervasive example is open source software (OSS), a global public good that plays a vital role in the economy and is foundational for most technology we use today. However, it is difficult to measure the value of OSS due to its non-pecuniary nature and lack of centralized usage tracking. Therefore, OSS remains largely unaccounted for in economic measures. Although prior studies have estimated the supply side costs to recreate this software, a lack of data has hampered estimating the much larger demand-side (usage) value created by OSS. Therefore, to understand the complete economic and social value of widely-used OSS, we leverage unique global data from two complementary sources capturing OSS usage by millions of global firms. We first estimate the supply-side value by calculating the cost to recreate the most widely used OSS once. We then calculate the demand side value based on a replacement value for each firm that uses the software and would need to build it internally if OSS did not exist. We estimate the supply-side value of widely-used OSS is $4.15 billion, but that the demand-side value is much larger at $8.8 trillion. We find that firms would need to spend 3.5 times more on software than they currently do if OSS did not exist. The top six programming languages in our sample comprise 84% of the demand-side value of OSS. Further, 96% of the demand-side value is created by only 5% of OSS developers.

# Raspberry Pi value surges past one billion on US buying

 Published: 05:58 27 Dec 2024 EST 

Raspberry Pi Holdings PLC (LSE:RPI) end-of-year charge continues with shares in the firm up a further 10% today a new all-time high of 658p.

Listed at 280p in July, the success of the DIY-PC maker’s short life on the London stock exchange is a counter to accusations that tech can’t work in London.

Recent buying by US investment group SW Investment Management is seemingly the reason behind the recent run, which has seen the share price double from 327p at the end of November.

A tightly held shareholder base is another reason, with well over 50% of the shares held by just two shareholders.

In September, the group reported underlying profits (EBITDA) of US$20.9 million, up by 55% from a year ago, on revenues up 61% to US$144 million. 

Sales volumes were marginally lower than expected, it said, though sales skewed towards higher margin variants. It noted that the same period a year ago was "supply-constrained".

The Pi 5 single-board computer (SBC), launched at the end of last October, sold 1.1 million units in the first half, with overall unit growth at 31%.

Shares jumped 60p to 658p, valuing the group at just under £1.3 billion.

## Abstract

Abstract How do barriers to the diffusion of academic research affect innovation? In 2008, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) mandated free online availability of funded research. This policy caused a 50 percentage point increase in free access to funded articles. We introduce a novel measure, in-text patent citations, to study how this mandate affected industry use of academic science. After 2008, patents cite NIH-funded research 12% to 27% more often. Nonfunded research, funded research in journals unaffected by the mandate, and academic citations see no change. These estimates are consistent with a model of search for useful knowledge. Inefficiency caused by academic publishing may be substantial.
